content: Amelanchier canadensis, commonly known as Canadian serviceberry, Juneberry, Shadblow Serviceberry, Shadbush, or Sugarplum, is a plant native to Canada and the United States. It is valued for its medicinal, culinary, and ornamental uses. This species is a medium-sized tree characterized by a tall, slender trunk and small, spreading branches that form a narrow, oblong crown. It is distributed throughout the eastern United States, extending southward to Florida and westward to Minnesota. The tree thrives in rich soils, particularly in upland woods, and reaches its largest size in the mountainous regions of North Carolina and Tennessee. Its roots are fibrous. The leaves of Amelanchier canadensis resemble those of a pear tree but are finer and more delicate. When emerging from the bud, they are covered in a soft, silken down, which becomes smooth as they mature. The leaves are alternate, simple, and ovate to ovate-oblong in shape, measuring three to four inches in length and one and a half to two inches in width. They are cordate or rounded at the base, serrate along the edges, and acute or acuminate at the tip. The leaves are feather-veined, with a grooved midrib on the upper surface and a prominent midrib on the underside. When they first emerge, they are reddish-brown and hairy, but they mature to a deep green color on the upper surface and a paler green beneath. In autumn, the leaves turn a bright yellow. The petioles are slender and grooved, while the stipules are lanceolate, downy, and shed early. The tree produces flowers in April, when the leaves are about one-third grown. The flowers are perfect, white, and borne in loose racemes that are three to five inches long. Each flower has a slender pedicel with two lanceolate, purplish, silky bractlets that fall off as the flower opens. The calyx is campanulate (bell-shaped) with five lanceolate, acute, downy, and persistent lobes that are imbricate in the bud. The corolla consists of five white, strap-shaped petals, each measuring half an inch to an inch in length, which are inserted on the calyx tube and imbricate in the bud. The stamens number twenty and are also inserted on the calyx tube. The filaments persist in the fruit, and the anthers are introrse, two-celled, with cells that open longitudinally. The pistil has an ovary that is twoto five-celled and united to the calyx tube. The styles, numbering two to five, have broad stigmas, and each cell of the ovary contains two ovules. Upon maturity, each cell is divided by a cartilaginous partition, resulting in ten cells, each containing one seed. The fruit of Amelanchier canadensis is a berry-like pome that is depressed-globular or pyriform in shape. It is open at the summit and crowned with the calyx lobes and remnants of the filaments. It is sweet and has a delicious flavor. The seeds are dark brown, with thick cotyledons. The fruit is highly regarded for its taste, but the yield is typically low, with even the largest trees rarely producing more than a quart of berries. Birds often consume most of the fruit. Native Americans valued the fruit highly. The tree is also admired for its ornamental qualities, being a flowering tree of exceptional elegance and beauty. It is often compared to other notable flowering trees such as the Carolina silverbell, the Dogwood, and the Eastern Redbud. The name Shad Bush was given to this tree by early settlers in the eastern United States because it blooms along tidal rivers at the same time that shad fish ascend these rivers to spawn.
